extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Shakespearean drama, literary historians, and advanced literature students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for assigning dates and periods to Shakespeare's plays (and related poems) using external documentary evidence, internal stylistic tests, and quantitative metrical measurements. Emphasises caution, corroboration, and the limits of each kind of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: External documentary evidence (records and title-pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documentary records such as entries in the Revels at Court, the Register of the Stationers' Company, and dates printed on title-pages of plays as direct evidence for dating and attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: performance records (e.g., Comedy of Errors at Gray's Inn, 1594), Stationers' Register entries, and title-page dates. Treat these as primary anchors for chronology but check authenticity and possible reprints or later title-page dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary diaries and eyewitness accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary diaries or eyewitness reports of performances can locate plays in time and place (e.g., Dr. Simon Forman's diary noting Globe performances in 1610–11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such firsthand observations are strong external evidence; verify reliability of the diarist and whether the entry refers to the play in its extant form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary references and lists by contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentions of Shakespeare and lists of his plays by contemporaries (e.g., Francis Meres' Palladis Tamia, 1598) serve as terminus ante quem / evidence of circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to show that certain works or sonnets existed by a given date. Check whether the reference is to manuscript circulation or printed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlets and topical material suggesting models or sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlets, travel accounts, or printed material that match plot-elements (e.g., Somers's voyage pamphlets and suggestions for The Tempest) are external clues to influence and possible dating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show likely sources and contexts; use with caution because influence need not be immediate and may indicate thematic borrowing rather than exact dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusions to contemporary personal or political events inside plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal allusions to current events (e.g., Prologue to Henry V referencing Essex’s expedition, 1599) can provide chronological markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such allusions are helpful for narrowing composition dates but require careful interpretation: some allusions may be topical satire, later interpolations, or ambiguous in reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusions to other books and inter-play references
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations or verbal echoes of other authors (e.g., Marlowe quoted in As You Like It) and references from one play to another (promises in epilogues) can date relative composition and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track literary borrowings and cross-references to establish sequence; beware of common clichés and conventional borrowing that do not indicate priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal moral and aesthetic considerations (subjective tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests based on perceived moral tone or aesthetic maturity of a play (e.g., perceived depth of feeling) are generally powerful to an individual reader but are subjective and hard to prove to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such judgments sparingly; they may suggest period but cannot stand alone as proof. Always corroborate with more objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and character-treatment analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination of methods used in plot construction and character development—considered less subjective than moral judgments—can indicate the maturity and period of the author’s technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for changes in complexity, psychological realism, and handling of dramatic types across plays to place works in relative sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features: classical allusions and Latin usages
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and nature of classical allusions, Latin words, and quotations are stylistic indicators that vary over an author's career and can aid period placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare frequency and sophistication of classical references across plays; consider the poet's exposure and the play's intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features: figures of speech, puns, conceits, and elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree and type of rhetorical ornament—puns, conceits, and elaboration—serve as stylistic markers that change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether language is ornate or concentrated; note that changes may reflect genre or scene-type as well as chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features: diffuseness vs concentration of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether expression is diffuse or concentrated can signal an earlier 'technical' stage or later maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider this alongside other style markers; isolated examples are not decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic features: artificiality vs lifelikeness in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which dialogue feels artificial or lifelike helps judge development in dramatic realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare dialogue across plays and scenes; genre conventions and intended comic/formal effects can influence this trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prose vs verse as a stylistic/functional indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's deployment of prose versus verse is informative: prose often used for low comedy or repartee, verse for high emotion or romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tavern scenes and comic servants often in prose; romantic moonlight scenes and emotional speeches in verse. Note: genre and scene purpose may override chronological signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment of oaths and statutory changes as dating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of certain social words or oaths (some later checked by statute after James I) can bracket a play’s composition historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal or statutory changes affecting language usage can serve as chronological markers; verify the dating of statutes and assess whether the text reflects original usage or later alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification tests (list of metrical features)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suite of metrical features—frequency of rhyme, doggerel lines, alexandrines, extra syllables before pauses, short lines, substitutions for strict iambic movement, weak/light line endings, position of pause (end-stopped vs run-on), feminine or hypermetrical endings—used as tests for relative dating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are more mechanical and quantifiable than many stylistic tests; analyze collectively rather than relying on any single feature. Beware that subject/atmosphere and revisions can affect meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of rhyme as chronological indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of rhymed lines (heroic couplets, alternate rhymes, sonnet arrangements) tends to be higher in earlier plays and declines in later works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High rhyme counts in plays like A Midsummer-Night's Dream and Romeo and Juliet may be genre-driven (lyrical tone). Do not count masque/vision/rhymed interludes when they are clearly separate forms unless appropriate to the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminine endings percentage trend (quantitative threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of pentameter lines with feminine (extra unstressed) endings increases over time: before c.1598 usually below 20%, afterwards commonly above 20% rising to ~35% in The Tempest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these percentage thresholds as a dating signal. Combine with other metrification measures; exceptions may occur due to revision or genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of pause: end-stopped vs run-on lines (and speeches ending within the line)
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing tendency toward run-on lines and pauses within the line (and an increase in speeches ending within the line) is characteristic of later plays and can be used as a chronological marker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify percentage of run-on lines and percentage of speeches ending within the line; compare with established patterns (e.g., low in Comedy of Errors, high in The Tempest). Scoring depends on consistent definitions of run-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of short lines, alexandrines, and substitutions in foot for stylistic/chronological evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of alexandrines (12-syllable lines), short lines at speech-ends, and substitutions of non-iambic feet are measurable features that vary historically and by genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider frequency and distribution; some forms (e.g., lyric passages, emotional outbursts) may intentionally employ these devices irrespective of chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light and weak line endings as a late-career signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of ending lines with light or weak words (prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries) was largely avoided earlier but becomes more common from about 1606 onward in Shakespeare's later plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure percentage of such endings; use with caution because cataloguing what counts as 'light' can be subjective and disputed among scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative metrical statistics (table metrics to be measured)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective metrics to be tabulated include total number of lines, number of prose lines, blank verse lines, pentameter rhymes, % blank verse with feminine endings, % run-on lines, % speeches ending within the line, and counts/percentages of light/weak endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables I–III in the text illustrate these measures. Use consistent counting methods and be aware that different scholars (Fleay, König, Ingram, Bradley) may produce differing figures; discrepancies require re-counting and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-driven uses of medium (prose/verse) limiting chronological inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific uses of prose or verse are often determined by dramatic function (low comedy, repartee, moralizing, romantic passages), so medium alone is not a reliable chronological indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret medium in context: scene function and character type may explain prose/verse choice irrespective of date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborated plays require separate treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays not wholly written by Shakespeare (collaborations) yield metrification and stylistic figures that are less significant for attributing authorial chronology and should be treated separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present collaborative plays in separate tables or analyses; avoid attributing aggregate metrics to Shakespeare alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of cuts, revisions, and editorial alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuts and revisions can leave broken lines and other artifacts that distort metrical counts (e.g., high percentages of run-on lines due to revisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for editorial history and textual corruptions when using metrical statistics; annotate where figures may be inflated by later changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of individual judgment and definitional clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many measures (what constitutes a run-on line, a light ending, etc.) involve borderline cases and scholarly disagreement, necessitating careful individual judgment and consistent definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document counting rules and be ready to reconcile differences with other scholars; significant discrepancies (as between Bradley and König) justify a re-count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metrification to corroborate, not to fix precise dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification and metrical tests corroborate external evidences and supplement them but cannot by themselves fix an exact year of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine external documents, topical allusions, stylistic tests, and numeric metrics to form a balanced chronology; avoid overconfidence based on one line of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro-classification into periods by dominant dramatic types
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify Shakespeare's career into periods based on shifts in predominant dramatic types (e.g., experimental early stage, triumph of comedy, period of great tragedies, late dramatic romances) as a way to understand chronological and stylistic development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this periodization as a heuristic summary synthesized from many evidences; recognize that period boundaries are approximate and causation may be multifactorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution: theatrical fashion and public taste as causal factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the kinds of plays Shakespeare wrote may reflect theatrical fashions, public taste, and available material as much as personal biography or immediate emotional experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining periodization, favor external cultural and market explanations over simple biographical reading-in; consider opportunity, demand, and innovations by other dramatists as influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dating of poems by stylistic parallels and publication/mention dates
rubrics_metrics.description: For poems (Venus and Adonis, Lucrece, Sonnets), use parallels to plays of certain periods and external evidence (e.g., Meres' 1598 mention, 1609 publication of Sonnets) to establish composition ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat shorelines: Venus and Adonis and Lucrece align with early dramatic practice; Sonnets likely composed over a period of years—use thematic depth and stylistic markers plus documentary mentions to infer chronology.
